messages.subject: Questions about user-defined functions
parts:

       bar[i] <- x[i]^(1.-r) / (1.-r);

> Two questions about user-defined functions:

> 1. If the function takes a vector argument, is there a way to get the length of the vector so I can loop over its elements? I would like to do something like this:

> }
> return(bar);
> }
>
> So as a work-around, I'm trying this to exponentiate a vector:
> vector foo(vector x, real r) {
> return exp(log(x) * (1. - r)) / (1. - r);
> }
>
> 2. I am having problems compiling .stan files with user-defined functions. The attached file compiles from .stan to .cpp with no complaints, but the c++ compiler gives me a long and confusing bunch of error messages, of which this seems most germane:

I isolated the bug and created a small reproducible example,
which I included in the issue along with an explanation:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/849

For now, you can workaround the bug with this modified function:

vector eu_item(vector x, real r) {
if (r == 1.) {
vector[cols(x)] log_x;
log_x <- log(x);
return log_x;
// WAS JUST: return log(x);
} else {
return exp(log(x) * (1.-r)) / (1.-r); # x^(1.-r) / (1.-r)
}

The problem arises in the "return log(x)" when x is data and
r is a parameter. The return scalar type for log(x) is double (data),
but it needs to be promoted to an autodiff variable (parameter).

This should be fixed by the next release.

Having said all this, I think there's going to be an issue with
your function, because if r is real, it should never be exactly 1,
as that's a measure 0 subset of the probability mass for it. So you
could probably just drop this altogether.

Are there constraints on what r's value should be? If r > 1, that
looks like it could be problematic.

- Bob

parts:
Thanks.

I was going to ask a followup about the "r=1" case, but wanted to test the code myself first.

This is a pretty standard utility function from economics, describing constant relative risk-aversion and plausible values span 1. The function is weird because what I really want is to know if f(x,r) > f(y,r) for some parameter r and data x: bernoulli_logit( scale * (f(x,r) - f(y,r))), where f(x,r) = x^(1-r) / (1-r) . But the function blows up near r=1 because it divides by zero. The special case for "r=1" is to avoid this singularity, and is the standard treatment in the econ literature. I probably should deal with the measure-zero issue by adjusting to use a neighborhood:

if (fabs(r=1.0) < epsilon)
  return log(x);
else
  return pow(x, 1.0 - r) / (1.0 - r);


r > 1 (x to a negative power) is not an issue because x >= 0  and I can avoid the x=0 case by adding a small number to make x strictly greater than 0.

If I could avoid r = 1, that would be nice, but the literature reports values that range from 0 to 40 or higher for different conditions and based on a lot of that literature, r=1 is a pretty reasonable mode for a prior.  A published MLE of the data set I'm working with gives a 95% CI of 0.67 to 1.02 for r.

How badly will this function screw up Stan's ability to calculate Jacobians? Do you have any suggestions for how to code something like this efficiently in Stan?

Maybe Michael will know.

I'm not sure where you mean. The only Jacobian (determinants) we compute
are for the transforms, and that doesn't depend on anything past the
parameters block.

It will screw up gradients at r = 1 as the function's discontinuous.
I'm not sure what happens under the crossing, because of the sign change.
With a fixed x and r = 1 + epsilon, you get a really big value, whereas
with a fixed x and r = 1 - epsilon, you get a really small value. So the
function's discontinuous at r, which is a problem. It's impossible to
simulate a particle moving according to the Hamiltonian when it has to
cross a discontinuous boundary. In fact, we want the derivatives to
be continuous, as well as the function (which is why fabs() can be problematic).

- Bob

parts:
Hi,

Maybe I missed something in the earlier discussion, but the
CRRA/isoelastic utility function family defined as

log(c) if r=1
(c^(1-r) - 1)/(1-r) otherwise

_is_ continuous both in c and r. The standard way of showing this is
using L'Hopital's rule. The -1 in the numerator is important, and seems
to be missing in the definition below.

The function is also continuously differentiable in c (u'(c)=c^(-r)),
and also in r --- this can be shown by calculating

\lim_{r\to1} \frac{(c^(1-r) - 1)/(1-r)-log(c)}{r-1} = -\log^2(c)/2

Best,

Tamas

parts:
Within the context of an (economic, not statistical) model, the CRRA
coefficient (r below) is usually fixed, and affine transformations don't
affect comparisons of utility, so it is common to drop the -1. But it is
needed for a continuous family. On top of that, economists rarely
consider differentiability in the coefficient, I had to do the proof for
continuity myself before posting, just to be sure.

I wonder if this solves the OP's problem.

Best,

Tamas

>>>>> 2. I am having problems compiling .stan files with user-defined functions. The attached file compiles from .stan to .cpp with no complaints, but the c++ compiler gives me a long and confusing bunch of error messages, of which this seems most germane:
>>>> I isolated the bug and created a small reproducible example,
>>>> which I included in the issue along with an explanation:
>>>>
>>>> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/849
>>>>
>>>> For now, you can workaround the bug with this modified function:
>>>>
>>>> vector eu_item(vector x, real r) {
>>>> if (r == 1.) {
>>>> vector[cols(x)] log_x;
>>>> log_x <- log(x);
>>>> return log_x;
>>>> // WAS JUST: return log(x);
>>>> } else {
>>>> return exp(log(x) * (1.-r)) / (1.-r); # x^(1.-r) / (1.-r)
>>>> }
>>>>
>>>> The problem arises in the "return log(x)" when x is data and
>>>> r is a parameter. The return scalar type for log(x) is double (data),
>>>> but it needs to be promoted to an autodiff variable (parameter).
>>>>
>>>> This should be fixed by the next release.
>>>>
>>>> Having said all this, I think there's going to be an issue with
>>>> your function, because if r is real, it should never be exactly 1,
>>>> as that's a measure 0 subset of the probability mass for it. So you
>>>> could probably just drop this altogether.
>>>>
>>>> Are there constraints on what r's value should be? If r > 1, that
>>>> looks like it could be problematic.
>>>>
>>>> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Questions about user-defined functions [& discontinuous functions/gradients]
parts:
Thanks for the pointer.

I wrote an initialization function in R that draws initial values from
my (weakly informative) priors, and then checks them for validity before
passing them to Stan. That seems to do the trick for the most part.

I still do get a few error messages from Stan in the early iterations
because something is over or underflowing and passing #IND values to
bernoulli_logit_log but once Stan has evaluated 100 or so samples, the
chains run with no further error messages, and looking at the traceplots
and density plots, it looks as though the chains mix nicely and don't
get stuck above or below 1, and with a few thousand samples, the
posterior density is smooth where it crosses 1 and Rhat for all the
parameters and lp__ are very close to 1.

Thanks for all the help and advice. Once I fixed the error Tamas pointed
out and got rid of the if statement, the stan computations sped up by a
couple of orders of magnitude (in effective samples per second).

Jonathan

> because it's a round number and looks near the value you're
> expecting.

>> -1 in the numerator. Thanks for catching my error.

>> With this, I should be able to write a function that will be fine
>> because the only problem is the measure-zero set (r=1) and the
>> probability of drawing a sample sufficiently close to r=1 to blow up the

>> On 8/12/2014 2:44 AM, Tamas Papp wrote:
>>> Hi,
>>>
>>> Maybe I missed something in the earlier discussion, but the
>>> CRRA/isoelastic utility function family defined as
>>>
>>> log(c) if r=1
>>> (c^(1-r) - 1)/(1-r) otherwise
>>>
>>> _is_ continuous both in c and r. The standard way of showing this is
>>> using L'Hopital's rule. The -1 in the numerator is important, and seems
>>> to be missing in the definition below.
>>>
>>> The function is also continuously differentiable in c (u'(c)=c^(-r)),
>>> and also in r --- this can be shown by calculating
>>>
>>> \lim_{r\to1} \frac{(c^(1-r) - 1)/(1-r)-log(c)}{r-1} = -\log^2(c)/2
>>>
>>> Best,
>>>
>>> Tamas

>>> On Mon, Aug 11 2014, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>>>> [expanded subject --- Michael see below]
>>>>
>>>> On Aug 10, 2014, at 5:40 PM, Jonathan Gilligan <jonathan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>>> Thanks.
>>>>>
>>>>> I was going to ask a followup about the "r=1" case, but wanted to test the code myself first.
>>>>>
>>>>> This is a pretty standard utility function from economics, describing constant relative risk-aversion and plausible values span 1. The function is weird because what I really want is to know if f(x,r) > f(y,r) for some parameter r and data x: bernoulli_logit( scale * (f(x,r) - f(y,r))), where f(x,r) = x^(1-r) / (1-r) . But the function blows up near r=1 because it divides by zero. The special case for "r=1" is to avoid this singularity, and is the standard treatment in the econ literature. I probably should deal with the measure-zero issue by adjusting to use a neighborhood:
>>>>>
>>>>> if (fabs(r=1.0) < epsilon)
>>>>> return log(x);
>>>>> else
>>>>> return pow(x, 1.0 - r) / (1.0 - r);
>>>>>
>>>> this has to be coded with "r == 1.0", but the compiler
>>>> will tell you that.
>>>>
>>>>> r > 1 (x to a negative power) is not an issue because x >= 0 and I can avoid the x=0 case by adding a small number to make x strictly greater than 0.
>>>> If you have a constraint lower=0 on x, then x will only be 0 if you initialize to
>>>> 0 (which is an error in most cases) or if there's an underflow.
>>>>
>>>>> If I could avoid r = 1, that would be nice, but the literature reports values that range from 0 to 40 or higher for different conditions and based on a lot of that literature, r=1 is a pretty reasonable mode for a prior. A published MLE of the data set I'm working with gives a 95% CI of 0.67 to 1.02 for r.
>>>>>
>>>>> How badly will this function screw up Stan's ability to calculate Jacobians? Do you have any suggestions for how to code something like this efficiently in Stan?
>>>> Maybe Michael will know.
>>>>
>>>> I'm not sure where you mean. The only Jacobian (determinants) we compute
>>>> are for the transforms, and that doesn't depend on anything past the
>>>> parameters block.
>>>>
>>>> It will screw up gradients at r = 1 as the function's discontinuous.
>>>> I'm not sure what happens under the crossing, because of the sign change.
>>>> With a fixed x and r = 1 + epsilon, you get a really big value, whereas
>>>> with a fixed x and r = 1 - epsilon, you get a really small value. So the
>>>> function's discontinuous at r, which is a problem. It's impossible to
>>>> simulate a particle moving according to the Hamiltonian when it has to
>>>> cross a discontinuous boundary. In fact, we want the derivatives to
>>>> be continuous, as well as the function (which is why fabs() can be problematic).
>>>>
>>>> - Bob
